title: Rental Property Tax Deductions Landlords Can Claim
metaDescription: Discover the top rental property tax deductions for landlords, including mortgage interest, depreciation, repairs, insurance, and mileage rules.
h1: Rental Property Tax Deductions for Landlords
cardBlurb: Learn which rental expenses reduce your taxable income, how depreciation works, and the reporting steps for Schedule E.
introText:
You can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses incurred to manage, conserve, and maintain your rental property, including mortgage interest, property taxes, operating costs, repairs, and annual depreciation. In the guides we publish on ModernWallet, we show property owners how tracking these deductible line items protects net cash flow from unnecessary tax burdens.

Rental property owners who report their income and expenses accurately can offset a substantial portion of their gross rent receipts. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) outlines these eligible categories under [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527), which governs residential rental property rules.

Every dollar in legitimate rental property tax deductions reduces your taxable net rental income for the tax year. Understanding the exact line between currently deductible operating costs and multi-year capitalized assets is the key to managing your real estate tax liability without triggering audit penalties.

sections.heading: Top Rental Property Tax Deductions
sections.body:
Every residential landlord can deduct operating expenses that are both ordinary and necessary for managing their real estate. Ordinary expenses are common and accepted in the rental business, while necessary expenses are appropriate and helpful for generating rental income.

The most common rental property tax deductions available to owners include:

- Mortgage interest paid on acquisition or improvement loans
- Annual residential building depreciation
- Local real estate property taxes
- Hazard, fire, and liability insurance premiums
- Routine maintenance and structural repairs
- Professional property management fees
- Legal, accounting, and tax preparation fees
- Business travel and vehicle mileage related to property management
- Utilities paid directly by the landlord
- Advertising costs, cleaning fees, and ordinary office supplies

These deductions apply to individuals holding residential property directly or through pass-through entities. If you run a property purely for personal vacation use without renting it to tenants, you cannot claim these business operating deductions.

sections.heading: Mortgage Interest Rules and Refinance Limits
sections.body:
Mortgage interest paid on a rental property loan is a deductible rental operating expense on your tax return. Because loan payments consist of both principal and interest, you must isolate the interest portion using the annual mortgage statement provided by your lender.

You cannot deduct the principal portion of your loan payment. Principal payments reduce loan debt rather than representing an operational cost, so only the financing fee and interest charges qualify for the deduction.

A common issue arises when landlords refinance an existing rental loan. If a refinance pulls out more than the previous loan balance, interest tied to the portion used for non-rental purposes is not deductible as a rental expense. If you use cash-out refinance proceeds to purchase personal assets, you must trace and separate the interest charges according to [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527).

sections.heading: Property Taxes and Insurance Premiums
sections.body:
Local property taxes assessed on your rental real estate are fully deductible in the year you pay them. These municipal taxes represent a direct operational cost of holding real estate for investment purposes.

Insurance premiums covering fire, theft, flood, and general liability for your rental units are also deductible expenses. Landlords frequently carry specialized landlord policies that protect against tenant property damage and loss of rental income.

The IRS enforces a strict timing rule when you prepay insurance coverage. If you purchase a prepaid multi-year policy, you must spread the deduction across the calendar years the policy covers. You cannot deduct the entire multi-year premium in the initial year you remit payment.

sections.heading: Repairs Versus Capital Improvements
sections.body:
The tax code draws a strict line between currently deductible repairs and multi-year capital improvements. Understanding this boundary protects you from misclassifying routine expenses or capitalizing costs that could lower your current tax bill.

Repairs keep your property in an ordinary, efficient operating condition without materially adding to its market value or extending its useful life. Routine maintenance tasks like fixing a roof leak, patching drywall, servicing a furnace, or repainting a room qualify as deductible expenses in the year paid.

Capital improvements include expenditures that better the property, restore an asset, or adapt it to a new use. Examples include installing a brand-new roof, building an addition, replacing all plumbing lines, or completing an extensive kitchen remodel. You must capitalize improvements and recover their cost over time through annual depreciation rather than expensing them immediately.

sections.heading: Rental Property Depreciation and Recapture Rules
sections.body:
Depreciation allows rental property owners to recover the purchase cost of the residential building over time. Land, however, never depreciates because it does not wear out or become obsolete, so you must allocate your initial purchase price between the physical building structure and the underlying parcel.

Residential rental buildings are depreciated using the straight-line method over a fixed 27.5-year recovery period under the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS). The IRS applies a mid-month convention, which treats property as placed in service in the middle of the month regardless of the exact closing date.

Tax deductions for rental property owners through depreciation create substantial paper losses, but that tax savings triggers a consequence when you sell. When a rental property is sold, the portion of the gain attributable to depreciation already claimed, known as unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, is taxed at a maximum federal rate of 25 percent under [IRS Publication 544](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p544). This rate applies separately from ordinary long-term capital gains rates on the remaining appreciation.

sections.heading: Travel and Transportation Expenses
sections.body:
Travel to your rental property to collect rent, inspect conditions, perform maintenance, or show units to prospective tenants is deductible. The primary purpose of the trip must be managing or maintaining your rental business rather than personal recreation.

For vehicle use, landlords can choose between deducting actual vehicle operating expenses or using the standard mileage rate. If you choose the standard mileage method, you must maintain an accurate written mileage log recording the date, destination, business mileage, and business purpose of every trip.

The IRS standard mileage rate for business use of a vehicle is 72.5 cents per mile for travel from January 1 through June 30, 2026. That rate rises to 76 cents per mile for travel from July 1 through December 31, 2026, as announced by the IRS in their [2026 business standard mileage rate notice](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-sets-2026-business-standard-mileage-rate-at-725-cents-per-mile-up-25-cents).

sections.heading: Legal Fees and Professional Services
sections.body:
Fees paid to attorneys, accountants, and investment advisors for rental operations represent deductible professional expenses. These expenses reduce net rental income when incurred directly to preserve or operate the rental property.

You can deduct legal fees paid to draft lease agreements, evict non-paying tenants, or defend property title claims. Similarly, bookkeeping services and accounting fees for ongoing rental financial management are deductible operating costs.

Tax preparation fees are also deductible for the portion of the return dedicated to the rental business. As stated in [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527), you can deduct legal and other professional expenses such as tax return preparation fees you paid to prepare Schedule E.

sections.heading: Utilities and Property Management Costs
sections.body:
Utilities that you pay on behalf of your tenants are fully deductible on your tax return. These include water, sewer, trash collection, natural gas, and electricity bills that the lease assigns to the owner.

If the tenant pays the utility company directly, you cannot claim a deduction for those utility charges. You may only deduct utility bills where you bear the financial obligation and make the direct payments.

Property management fees paid to a third-party management company or leasing agent are also deductible operating costs. In addition, you can deduct the cost of advertising vacant units, tenant background check fees, cleaning supplies, and ordinary office supplies used in your rental operation.

sections.heading: Filing Schedule E and the Safe Harbor Election
sections.body:
Landlords report rental real estate income and deduct operating expenses on [Schedule E (Form 1040)](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-schedule-e-form-1040), Supplemental Income and Loss. Each residential property gets reported in a separate column detailing total rent received and itemized expenses.

Annual building depreciation is calculated on [Form 4562](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-4562) and then transferred directly to Schedule E. Maintaining clean accounting records throughout the year ensures each line item matches IRS categories and expedites the preparation of both forms.

A de minimis safe harbor election allows landlords to expense lower-cost tangible items immediately rather than capitalizing and depreciating them over multiple years. This election applies to qualifying small purchases up to a specific per-item or per-invoice threshold outlined in the [IRS Tangible Property Regulations](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/tangible-property-final-regulations). Check the IRS guidance directly to confirm the current dollar limit before filing your annual election statement.

sections.heading: Tax Management Tips for Rental Owners
sections.body:
We see property owners leave substantial money on the table when they fail to log minor expenses throughout the operating year. Tracking small out-of-pocket purchases like hardware store receipts and maintenance mileage consistently prevents write-offs from slipping through the cracks.

Maintain separate bank accounts and credit cards exclusively for each rental property or rental business entity. Commingling personal and business finances makes auditing Schedule E line items difficult and increases accounting fees during tax season.

Landlords operating multiple units often evaluate their operating margins against broader industry standards. Across real estate investing, operating costs frequently consume 40% to 50% of gross rental income as a general rule of thumb, which reinforces the need to capture every legitimate deduction. You can test your property margins and estimate tax liability using our [rental income tax calculator](/real-estate/rental-income-tax-calculator/).

Plan ahead for eventual property dispositions by monitoring accumulated depreciation from the first year in service. When you sell, unrecaptured depreciation will be taxed, so factoring in that future liability prevents surprises when calculating your true net profit. Review our [tax deductions checklist](/guides/tax-deductions-checklist/) to organize your rental records before submitting your next tax filing.

faqs.question: What is the biggest tax deduction for rental property owners?
faqs.answer: Depreciation is typically the largest tax deduction for rental property owners because it allows you to deduct the cost of the building structure over 27.5 years without spending cash each year. Combined with mortgage interest and local property taxes, depreciation often offsets a large percentage of taxable rental income.

faqs.question: Can I deduct mortgage interest on a rental property?
faqs.answer: Yes, mortgage interest paid on a loan used to acquire or improve your rental property is fully deductible on Schedule E. However, if you complete a cash-out refinance and use a portion of the funds for personal expenses, interest on that personal portion is not deductible as a rental expense.

faqs.question: Is a new roof on a rental property tax deductible right away?
faqs.answer: No, a new roof is considered a capital improvement that restores or betters the property, so you must capitalize and depreciate the cost over 27.5 years. By contrast, minor repairs like patching a small roof leak or replacing broken shingles are deductible immediately in the year paid.

faqs.question: Do I need receipts to claim rental property tax deductions?
faqs.answer: Yes, you should retain receipts, bank statements, invoices, and mileage logs for all claimed expenses to satisfy IRS substantiation standards. If the IRS examines your tax return, documentary evidence is required to verify that the expenses were ordinary, necessary, and actually paid.

faqs.question: What happens to depreciation when I sell a rental property?
faqs.answer: When you sell a rental property, the IRS recaptures the depreciation deductions you claimed or could have claimed during ownership. This unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is taxed at a maximum federal rate of 25 percent, separate from ordinary capital gains rates on the remaining property appreciation.
